extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing USPTO patent-eligibility analyses under the MPEP (Step 2A/2B), including identification of judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural phenomena, products of nature) and the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting/analyzing/displaying/manipulating information (abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to concepts such as collecting, displaying, manipulating, analyzing, recognizing, and storing information are abstract ideas (e.g., data collection, recognition and storage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: Alice (claims requiring a computer that processed streams of bits found abstract); FairWarning (collecting access information, applying rules to detect misuse, and notifying users found to be an abstract idea); other cited examples include: (i) collecting, displaying, and manipulating data (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One); (ii) collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (iii) creating an index and using it to search/retrieve data (Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem.); (iv) determining a price using organizational/product hierarchies (Versata v. SAP); (v) encoding and decoding image data (RecogniCorp v. Nintendo); (vi) organizing information through mathematical correlations (Digitech Image Techs. v. Electronics for Imaging); (vii) relaying mailing address data (Return Mail, Inc. v. USPS); (viii) retaining information in navigation of online forms (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). The Office treats these kinds of information-processing concepts as abstract ideas in Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts having no particular concrete or tangible form (idea abstraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a combination of steps constituting an idea with no particular concrete or tangible form are directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ultramercial (an eleven-step method for displaying an ad in exchange for access to copyrighted media — characterized as 'an idea, having no particular concrete or tangible form' described as 'using advertising as an exchange or currency'); Versata (determining price using hierarchies described as a building block/basic conceptual framework); In re Brown (method of allocating hair weight described as the abstract idea of assigning hair designs to balance head shape). Such claims are treated as abstract ideas and evaluated under Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships/formulas (judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts — including mathematical algorithms, relationships, formulas, and calculations — are identified as judicial exceptions (abstract ideas) and are non-statutory subject matter unless applied in a patent-eligible manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have characterized formulas and algorithms (e.g., Benson: converting binary-coded decimal to binary; Flook: formula for computing an alarm limit; Mackay Radio: formula describing standing waves; Bilski: mathematical formula for hedging) as exceptions. Diamond v. Diehr noted that a mathematical formula (Arrhenius equation) is an exception like a scientific principle or law of nature. The Office treats such mathematical relationships/formulas as abstract ideas for Step 2A, requiring further Step 2B analysis to determine whether the claim recites a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing mathematical calculations (abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are essentially directed to performing mathematical calculations or manipulating mathematical results are considered directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bancorp (claims for managing life insurance policies by performing calculations and manipulating results were seen as the abstract idea of managing such a policy by computation); Digitech (claims generating and manipulating data using mathematical formulas and organizing the information into a new form were directed to organizing information through mathematical correlations). The Office looks to the specification and claimed steps to determine whether the claimed subject matter is mere mathematical computation and thus an abstract idea under Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (judicial exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (including naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that do not have markedly different characteristics) are judicial exceptions and are not patentable by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts view basic tools of scientific and technological work as not patentable. Examples identified as laws of nature/natural phenomena include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations between genetic variations and alleles, metabolic correlations (Mayo), presence of biomarkers correlated with disease (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism (O’Reilly v. Morse), qualities of bacteria (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry Genetics), chemical principles (Tilghman v. Proctor), and existence of cffDNA (Ariosa v. Sequenom). The guidance notes that not every claim describing a natural ability or response is directed to a law of nature (e.g., treatment methods applying a principle may be eligible). A claim that recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon is Step 2A: YES and requires Step 2B analysis to determine whether there is a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature (judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical products that are naturally occurring, or non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts, are products of nature and are exceptions to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: isolated DNA and cDNA (Myriad), cloned farm animals (Roslin), primers (Ambry), and similar illustrations. The guidance emphasizes that synthetic or human-made products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts remain products of nature. The Office treats 'product of nature' exceptions inclusively under Step 2A and instructs examiners to use the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to determine whether a claimed nature-based product limitation is an exception. If a claim to a nature-based product is broad enough under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to encompass unmarkedly-different embodiments that are products of nature, examiners should consider pointing out the BRI and recommending narrowing amendments where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (how and when to apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares a claimed nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether the product possesses markedly different characteristics (structure, function, and/or other properties). This analysis is part of Step 2A to identify product-of-nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and procedures: - Purpose: If a nature-based product has markedly different characteristics, it is not a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO) and may not require Step 2B unless another exception is recited. If it lacks markedly different characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and Step 2B is required. - Scope: Apply the analysis only to nature-based product limitations in the claim (not to non-nature-based claim elements). For claims to a nature-based product by itself, analyze the entire product. For a nature-based combination (multiple components), analyze the resultant nature-based combination. For a claim including a nature-based product plus non-nature-based elements, analyze only the nature-based product limitation; additional elements are evaluated in Step 2B. - Product-by-process: Determine whether the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (see MPEP §2113). - Process claims: Generally, do not apply the markedly different analysis to process claims because the focus is on active process steps, not products used; however, if a process claim is drafted such that it is substantively indistinguishable from a product claim (i.e., effectively claims the product), then apply the analysis to the recited nature-based product. - Selecting counterparts: Compare the nature-based product to the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state (e.g., for a derivative chemical, compare to the original natural chemical; for a nucleic acid derived from a gene, compare to that gene strand). When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart. - Characteristics for analysis: Consider structure, function, and other properties; evaluate on a case-by-case basis using what is recited in the claim and the specification. - Practical note: If the claimed nature-based product is by definition naturally occurring, no analysis beyond recognizing it is necessary. Examiners should consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06) is appropriate for claims that recite nature-based products but clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception.
